autocorrelation.simple: How strongly a series is related to its own past values.
autocorrelation.example: If today's temperature is close to yesterday's, the series has high autocorrelation.

cross-sectional.simple: Data about many things at one moment in time.
cross-sectional.example: The height of 1,000 people measured today.

panel data.simple: Data about many things, each measured at many moments. It is many time series in one table.

frequency.simple: The size of the time step of a series.

irregular time series.simple: A series whose time steps are not equal, such as a log of events.
irregular time series.example: The exact times when customers buy something.

trend.simple: The long-run direction of a series: going up, going down, or flat.
trend.example: The number of app users grows every year.

seasonality.simple: A pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period.
seasonality.example: Sales are high every Saturday (period 7 days).

cycle.simple: Rises and falls that repeat but with no fixed length.

noise.simple: The random part of a series that no model can predict.
noise.example: Small day-to-day changes caused by luck.

least squares.simple: A way to fit a line: choose the line that makes the sum of squared gaps to the data as small as possible.

additive model.simple: A model where the parts are added: y = trend + season + noise.
additive model.example: Swings of the season keep the same size at all levels.

multiplicative model.simple: A model where the parts are multiplied: y = trend × season × noise.
multiplicative model.example: Summer sales are 20% above normal, so swings grow with the level.

downsampling.simple: Changing a series to a coarser time step by combining rows, for example hourly to daily.

upsampling.simple: Changing a series to a finer time step. New rows have no data until you fill them.
upsampling.example: Monthly data turned into daily data with ffill.
